chapter.notes: Chapter covers aller, immediate future, venir, immediate past, tenir, faire, causative form, weather expressions, and vocabulary for days, months, seasons.

Wherever you want to go, you’ll need the verb aller (to go). It is an -er irregular verb, also used in many idiomatic expressions.
Use the preposition à (to, at, in) to say where you are going. Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.
Aller is also used to form the immediate future. So, to talk about what you are going to do, use aller in the present indicative followed immediately by a verb in the infinitive.
The verb venir (to come) and its derivatives, devenir (to become), prévenir (to warn, to inform), survenir (to occur), are all commonly used verbs.
The verb venir (to come) in the present tense + de, combined with a verb in the infinitive, expresses an action that has just taken place.
Another verb conjugated like venir is tenir (to hold)

grammar_rules.summary: Use the preposition à after aller to indicate destination; note contraction with le/les.
grammar_rules.explanation: The verb aller (to go) is followed by the preposition à to say where one is going. When à is followed by the definite articles le or les, they contract to au and aux respectively.
grammar_rules.formation: aller + à + place; à + le = au; à + les = aux
usage: To express going to a place.
restrictions: Only applies to destinations that require à; some places may use en or other prepositions.
exceptions: No contraction with la or l'.
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + aller conjugated + pas + à + place
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + aller conjugated + à + place? or inversion

attestations.source_text: Use the preposition à (to, at, in) to say where you are going. Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.

grammar_rules.summary: Formed with present tense of aller + infinitive; expresses near future; can replace present or future in colloquial speech.
grammar_rules.explanation: To talk about what you are going to do, use aller in the present indicative followed immediately by a verb in the infinitive. This construction can replace the present in colloquial speech and is often used as a substitute for the future tense in everyday conversation.
usage: To replace present or future in colloquial speech.
restrictions: Only used with present indicative of aller.
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + aller conjugated + infinitive? or inversion
common_traps: Using present instead of infinitive after aller.

attestations.source_text: Aller is also used to form the immediate future. So, to talk about what you are going to do, use aller in the present indicative followed immediately by a verb in the infinitive.
This construction can replace the present in colloquial speech.

grammar_rules.summary: venir (present) + de + infinitive expresses an action that has just taken place.
grammar_rules.explanation: Although the construction venir de is in the present tense in French, it conveys an idea in the past in English (just did something).
usage: To express an action that just occurred.
restrictions: Only with present tense of venir.
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + venir conjugated + pas + de + infinitive
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + venir conjugated + de + infinitive? or inversion

attestations.source_text: The verb venir (to come) in the present tense + de, combined with a verb in the infinitive, expresses an action that has just taken place.

grammar_rules.summary: tenir à means to be attached to something or to insist on doing something.
grammar_rules.explanation: When used with the preposition à, tenir means to be attached to (someone or something) or to insist on (doing something).
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + tenir conjugated + pas + à + object/infinitive
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + tenir conjugated + à + object/infinitive?

attestations.source_text: When used with the preposition à or de, tenir takes on another meaning. Elle tient à ses bijoux. She is attached to her jewels. Ils tiennent à leurs habitudes. They are attached to their habits. Marc tient à vous voir. Marc insists on seeing you.

grammar_rules.summary: tenir de means to take after someone.
grammar_rules.explanation: tenir de + person means to resemble or take after that person.
usage: To express resemblance to a family member.
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + tenir conjugated + pas + de + person
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + tenir conjugated + de + person?

attestations.source_text: De qui tient-elle? Whom does she take after? Elle tient de sa mère. She takes after her mother.

grammar_rules.summary: The verb faire is used in many expressions related to household chores, activities, and sports.
grammar_rules.explanation: Faire is commonly used with a definite article and a noun to express performing an activity (e.g., faire les courses, faire du vélo).
usage: To talk about chores, hobbies, sports.
grammar_rules.negative_form: ne + faire conjugated + pas + article + noun
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + faire conjugated + article + noun?
common_traps: Using jouer instead of faire for some activities.

attestations.section_title: The verb faire (to do, to make)
attestations.source_text: Faire is also used in expressions relating to chores, activities, sports, etc.

grammar_rules.summary: Use impersonal il + faire + adjective to describe weather.
grammar_rules.explanation: Faire is used with the impersonal third-person singular il in most expressions relating to the weather, e.g., il fait beau, il fait froid.
exceptions: Some weather conditions use other verbs: il pleut, il neige, il grêle, il bruine.
common_traps: Using faire for verbs like pleuvoir.

grammar_rules.summary: Some weather conditions use specific impersonal verbs: pleuvoir, neiger, grêler, bruiner.
grammar_rules.explanation: A few verbs relating to the weather are used in the impersonal il form, without faire: il pleut, il neige, il grêle, il bruine.

attestations.section_title: The verb faire (to do, to make)
attestations.source_text: A few verbs relating to the weather are used in the impersonal il form, without faire. Il pleut. It is raining. Il neige. It is snowing. Il grêle. It is hailing. Il bruine. It is drizzling.

grammar_rules.summary: Use faire + infinitive to express having something done or causing something to happen.
grammar_rules.explanation: The causative form is formed with the verb faire followed by an infinitive. It expresses the idea of having something done by someone or causing something to happen.
usage: To have something done by someone else.
exceptions: The agent may be introduced by par or à.
agreement_rules: The past participle of faire in compound tenses is invariable.
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + faire conjugated + infinitive?
transformations: Active sentence: Elle écrit la lettre. -> Causative: Elle fait écrire la lettre par sa secrétaire.
common_traps: Confusing causative with simple faire + noun.

attestations.source_text: It is formed with the verb faire followed by an infinitive.

grammar_rules.rule_name: Immediate future as substitute for future simple
grammar_rules.summary: In everyday conversation, the immediate future is often used as a substitute for the future tense (le futur simple).
grammar_rules.explanation: The immediate future can replace the future simple in colloquial speech without significant change in meaning.
grammar_rules.formation: Instead of future simple, use aller + infinitive.
usage: To express future actions in an informal register.
grammar_rules.interrogative_form: Est-ce que + subject + aller conjugated + infinitive?
common_traps: Overusing future simple in informal contexts.

attestations.source_text: And in everyday conversation, the immediate future is often used as a substitute for the future tense (le futur simple).

grammar_rules.summary: Aller is used in many common expressions such as Ça va?, Comment allez-vous?, etc.
grammar_rules.explanation: Aller appears in several common idiomatic expressions to ask about well-being or comment on appearance.

attestations.source_text: Aller is used in many common expressions.

grammar_rules.summary: devenir, prévenir, survenir, revenir are conjugated like venir.
grammar_rules.explanation: The derivatives of venir follow the same conjugation pattern as venir.
usage: To express becoming, warning, occurring, returning.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Contraction of à + le/les
exceptions_and_traps.description: Remember that à + le = au and à + les = aux, but no contraction with la or l'.

attestations.source_text: Watch out for the contraction: à + le = au and à + les = aux.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Immediate future vs future simple
exceptions_and_traps.description: In everyday conversation, the immediate future often replaces the future simple. Learners may overuse the future simple in informal contexts.

attestations.source_text: And in everyday conversation, the immediate future is often used as a substitute for the future tense (le futur simple).

exceptions_and_traps.title: Tenir à vs tenir de
exceptions_and_traps.description: tenir à means to be attached to or insist on; tenir de means to take after. They are easily confused.
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: using à instead of de or vice versa

attestations.source_text: When used with the preposition à or de, tenir takes on another meaning.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Faire weather vs impersonal verbs
exceptions_and_traps.description: Most weather descriptions use il fait + adjective, but some specific conditions use il pleut, il neige, il grêle, il bruine. Do not use faire with these verbs.
exceptions_and_traps.correct_form: il fait beau/froid/chaud; il pleut; il neige; il grêle; il bruine
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: il fait pleut, il fait neige, etc.

attestations.section_title: The verb faire (to do, to make)
attestations.source_text: A few verbs relating to the weather are used in the impersonal il form, without faire.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Causative vs simple faire + noun
exceptions_and_traps.description: The causative form uses faire + infinitive, not faire + noun. Example: faire faire la robe (have the dress made) vs faire la robe (make the dress).
exceptions_and_traps.incorrect_form: faire + noun when causative is intended

attestations.source_text: Elle fait la robe. She is making the dress. Elle fait faire la robe. She is having the dress made.
